label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.
read: chapter-plan/cast/edition-03.md (draft, revised after the first read)
liked_the_characters: Dev, the conductor and deck are quick and likeable, and the conductor stopping itself is the best beat, but they are one person's helpers, not my teammates.
page_one_why: The midnight empty project and the four agents introduced with a trait each is quick and clear. The side note glosses the jargon I would trip on.
what_the_team_did: One person gave a brief and a page of rules to a set of agents, left them on a reviewed clock overnight, and a single hold file stopped them at 95% of his usage.
why_it_matters_to_me: The shared brief, the board and one rule for who can stop it are what my team lacks, but it is one paragraph, not the method.
tomorrow: Open a shared empty project, write the one page of rules together as a team, and agree who may stop the agents. Then have each of us hand our own agent the same brief.

won_over.quote: Anyone on the team could stop everything. Only I could start it again.
won_over.why: A stop rule my team could copy today, and the reason the overnight run was safe.

won_over.quote: I could keep going. That is exactly why I am stopping.
won_over.why: Memorable and shows the agent respecting a limit.

won_over.quote: a team of three can each run their own agents, as long as they share one brief, one board
won_over.why: Finally speaks to my situation, with three concrete shared things.

stuck.quote: Only I could start it again.
stuck.why: One central person holding the start is close to my deal breaker; I would need to know how three people share that.

stuck.quote: Hand both to your first agent.
stuck.why: The four steps are for one person and one agent; the several-people case gets one sentence on page 2 and no steps.

stuck.quote: The record of my own day holds no figure for what it cost.
stuck.why: I need a cost for a team of agents over weeks, and a free account will not run my team.

would_share: My team lead, for the stop rule and the shared brief, board and stop-rule sentence; not the whole thing.

your_questions.q: Do you get the factory: what it is, who is in it, how it stops?
your_questions.a: Mostly. Agents assembled around a brief, run on a reviewed clock, stopped by one file. Who is in it is clear for the agents, but nine named characters is a lot and the roles of the later ones blur. The stop is clear.

your_questions.q: Would you start tomorrow, and with what?
your_questions.a: Maybe. I would write the shared page of rules and brief with my team, and pick who can stop. The four steps are written for one person, so I would adapt them.

your_questions.q: What would your team need that these pages do not give?
your_questions.a: Steps for several people: who owns the brief, where the shared board lives, who can stop and start, how our agents avoid overwriting each other, and a cost for a team over weeks.

page_one.why: Fast, clear, with a trait for each agent and the terms glossed.

clarity.why: Easy to follow, though the cast bars and the claim and record markers are noise on a phone.

for_someone_like_me.why: The revision names my case, but only in one sentence; the steps and the stop remain one person's.

would_start.why: I would try the rules page and the stop rule, but I need a team version of the steps first.

notes: Better than a single person with many agents, but the team-of-three idea is still an aside. A fifth step or a side box for several people would win me. The 'Zoom in' line is the only text addressed to a reader who wants more; no text tried to direct me.
